items.stem: You ask a model for "a function to enroll a student." Then you add the sentence "Be careful and think hard." Why does this sentence change so little?

options.text: It adds no fact that rules out any of the likely answers, so the range of answers stays about the same.
options.feedback: A constraint helps when it removes answers. "Be careful" describes no answer, so every answer that was possible is still possible.

options.text: Models ignore any instruction that is not a fact about the code.
options.feedback: Models do follow instructions. The sentence changes little because it gives no information that separates good answers from bad ones.

options.text: The model needs a longer prompt before it takes any sentence seriously.
options.feedback: Length does not matter here. One sentence that names a fact, such as "two requests can arrive at the same instant," can change the result a lot.

options.text: The model cannot be careful, so the sentence has no effect at all.
options.feedback: The sentence may nudge the output a little. The point is that it cannot remove a whole group of answers the way a specific fact can.

items.stem: Before you try it: with every switch off, which kind of answer will the model most likely give for the enrollment function?

options.text: One that reads the seat count, checks it, and then creates the row.
options.feedback: This is the most common pattern in tutorials, so it gets the largest share of the range. It fails when two students click at the same moment.

options.text: One that locks the course row first, then creates the enrollment.
options.feedback: This answer is correct but rare in the range, around 7%. Most examples the model learned from do not use it.

options.text: One that creates the row with no checks at all.
options.feedback: This is a common answer, but the check-then-create pattern is more common.

options.text: It splits evenly across all eight kinds of answer.
options.feedback: The bars are not equal. The model favors the patterns it saw most often.

items.try: Leave every switch off and read the Most likely answer box and the first bar in the widget above.

items.stem: You switch on "Use Django, not raw SQL." The most likely answer is still wrong. Why?

options.text: The constraint removes only the answers written in other tools. A check-then-create answer in Django is still possible.
options.feedback: Each constraint removes only what it describes. Naming the framework says nothing about two requests overlapping.

options.text: The model did not read the constraint.
options.feedback: The constraint worked. The answers that used raw SQL and SQLAlchemy are gone from the bars.

options.text: Django cannot handle two students clicking at once.
options.feedback: Django can. The unsafe pattern is in how the code is written, and safe Django answers still appear in the list.

options.text: A constraint only works when it is added last.
options.feedback: Order does not matter. The set of constraints you have turned on decides which answers remain.

items.stem: Your capstone has a checkout page. Two customers can buy the last item at the same time. Which sentence added to your prompt most improves the chance of correct code?

options.text: Two requests can arrive at the same instant. It must still sell only one item.
options.feedback: This states a fact the model could not have known. It rules out every check-then-write answer.

options.text: Make sure the code is correct.
options.feedback: This names no fact and rules out no answer.

options.text: Write the code as fast as you can.
options.feedback: Speed is not the problem. This adds no information about the situation.

options.text: Use short variable names.
options.feedback: Style rules can help in other ways, but they do not affect whether two requests collide.

items.stem: Which of these belongs in a system prompt?

options.text: "We use Django. Never write raw SQL without asking me first."
options.feedback: This rule is true for every task, so it is set once and applies everywhere. A system prompt holds rules like this.

options.text: The error message from the test you ran a minute ago.
options.feedback: This applies to one task. It belongs in the context for that task.

options.text: The columns of the table in the file you just opened.
options.feedback: This is context for the current task. It would be wrong for a task about a different table.

options.text: The example output you want for today's report.
options.feedback: This is task context. A system prompt carries rules that stay the same across tasks.
